grade.first_issue: Section 4 falsely asserts that recursive play can produce only repeated halvings of existing angles or of 90°. The one-move characterization does not imply this restriction for multi-move strategies.
grade.summary: The claimed classification omits valid values, so Rule A caps the score at 2. In particular, θ=60° is forceable. Every triangle has an angle c≤60°. If c=60°, Mulan has already won. Otherwise, write the other angles as a≥b and cut from the vertex of angle a so that the children have angle sets {b,60°,120°−b} and {c,120°,60°−c}. The cut is valid; the first child contains 60°, while in the second Mulan bisects the 120° angle, putting 60° in both resulting children. Thus 60° is a direct counterexample to the submitted classification. Repairing the proof requires fundamentally extending both the construction and the obstruction argument to obtain all θ=180°/n.
strengths: The analysis of when both immediate children can contain θ is substantially correct under the stated assumption that neither inherited base angle already equals θ.
The construction for θ=90° and the repeated angle-bisection argument correctly prove the dyadic subfamily θ=180°/2^n.

errors.description: The final answer is false: it excludes θ=60° and, more generally, all 180°/n with n not a power of two.

The necessity argument assumes without proof—and incorrectly—that every recursively forceable angle must arise by halving an existing angle or 90°. Multi-stage branching strategies allow other transformations, so the proposed invariant is invalid.
